messages.author: a89255530e96e85a
messages.subject: Generate categorical random variable as matrix index
parts:
I have code below that compiles / executes which I need to alter to correctly implement my model.
  
Specifically, the code below compiles/executes, based on a trivial coding of the indices of the ordTheta matrix, i.e.,

            ordTheta[1,2]

The ordTheta matrix is 2x3 and obviously this will always select the entry in the first row, second column.

In fact I need to reference the row (column) of the ordTheta matrix by a realization of a categorical RV whose parameter vector is the pi (pj) simplex associated with that row (column). 

To illustrate, the index values could be expressed as:

             piRow[n] <- categorical_rng(pi[n])
      pjCol[d] <- categorical_rng(pj[d])

Note, I realize that I can generate random numbers only in the generated quantities block, however I hoping there is another way to arrive at these values. I've tried various approaches and all have been unsuccessful.

If anyone has any suggestion(s) as to how I could do this I'd be extremely grateful!

Thanks so much,
Joe


data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> D;
  int<lower=1> K;
  int<lower=1> L;
  int<lower=0, upper=1> x[N,D];
  vector[K] alpha1;
  vector[L] alpha2;
}

parameters {
  matrix<lower=0, upper=1>[K,L] theta;
  simplex[K] pi[N];
  simplex[L] pj[D];
}


transformed parameters {
  matrix[N,K] log_pi;
  matrix[D,L] log_pj;
  vector[K*L] thetaVecSort;
  matrix[K,L] ordTheta;

  thetaVecSort <- sort_asc(to_vector(theta));

  for (n in 1:N)
    for (k in 1:K)
      log_pi[n,k] <- log(pi[n,k]);
 
  for (d in 1:D)
    for (l in 1:L)
      log_pj[d,l] <- log(pj[d,l]);

  ordTheta[1] <- transpose(segment(thetaVecSort,1,3));
  ordTheta[2] <- transpose(segment(thetaVecSort,4,3));

}

model {
      for(k in 1:K)                   
        for(l in 1:L)
           theta[k,l] ~ beta(1,1);
      for (n in 1:N){
              pi[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha1);
     }
      for (d in 1:D) {
             pj[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha2);
     }
      for (n in 1:N) {
         for (d in 1:D) {
                increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(x[n,d], ordTheta[1,2]));  // Would like to replace 1,2 in this line;
        }
     }
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Generate categorical random variable as matrix index
parts:
The model can't be coded directly in Stan because there
are no categorical parameters and the categorical_rng is intentionally
restricted to generated quantities to prevent users from trying
to use it in models. It breaks both the basic model concept (specification
of log probabilty up to an additive constant) and our main sampling
and optimization techniques, both of which rely on gradients.

You should, on the other hand, be able to marginalize out the
categorical variables. Check out the manual chapter on mixture
models for examples.

- Bob

I believe you mean something like this:

model {
      for(k in 1:K)                    
        for(l in 1:L)
           theta[k,l] ~ beta(1,1); 
      for (n in 1:N) 
         pi[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha1);
      for (d in 1:D) 
         pj[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha2);
      for (n in 1:N) { 
         for (d in 1:D) {

for (k in 1:K) {
             for (l in 1:L) {
                increment_log_prob(log_pi[n,k] + log_pj[d,l] + bernoulli_log(x[n,d], ordTheta[k,l]));
              }
           }
        }
     }
}


This is not the same as the model I'd like to estimate however as evidenced by the results (I've run this one previously). Specifically what in the model are the row (column) segment probabilities, pi (pj) have uniform resultant distributions, e.g. 2 row segments have .5 probability each and 3 column segments have .33 probability each. Results from JAGS based on the alternative likelihood do not result in uniform distributions so I'm assuming this is where the issue lies. 

If anyone has an alternative way of marginalizing out the categorical indicators for the ordTheta matrix, I really appreciate any suggestions.

- Joe

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Generate categorical random variable as matrix index
parts:
On Jun 17, 2014, at 10:08 PM, Retzer Joe <retz...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Jun 17, 2014, at 1:40 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>> You should, on the other hand, be able to marginalize out the
>> categorical variables. Check out the manual chapter on mixture
>> models for examples.
>
> I believe you mean something like this:
>
> model {
> for(k in 1:K)
> for(l in 1:L)
> theta[k,l] ~ beta(1,1);
> for (n in 1:N)
> pi[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha1);
> for (d in 1:D)
> pj[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha2);
> for (n in 1:N) {
> for (d in 1:D) {
> for (k in 1:K) {
> for (l in 1:L) {
> increment_log_prob(log_pi[n,k] + log_pj[d,l] + bernoulli_log(x[n,d], ordTheta[k,l]));
> }
> }
> }
> }
> }

At the level of the mixture, you need to add on the linear
scale, which means you need to do log_sum_exp on the log
scale. That is, you need to add probabilities a and b
on the linear scale to marginalize, which corresponds to:

log(a + b) = log_sum_exp(log(a), log(b))

where

log_sum_exp(x,y) = log(exp(x) + exp(y))

And there's a version that takes a vector argument, not just
binary. Check out the chapter in the manual.

- Bob
